title: Northstar Med on-prem airgapped discovery

Share air-gapped installer/upgrade flow doc + signed package process

Provide preliminary capacity estimate and cost for 3-rack on-prem pilot by EOD Friday
Prepare demo VM of private control plane screenshots and RBAC examples
action_items: Lena Zhou: Email SOC2 + network diagrams (2026-08-07)
Marcus Patel: Prepare air-gapped installer checklist and offline update flow doc (2026-08-07)
Tom Rivera: Share constrained power/cooling rack specs and expected QPS for pilot (2026-08-10)
Priya Singh: Confirm required encryption standards (FIPS/HSM) and compliance questions (2026-08-09)
summary: Discovery call focused on Northstar's requirements for an on-prem, air-gapped deployment of Redwood Private. Key discussion points: network isolation, offline signed updates, hardware constraints (power/cooling, preferred GPUs), compliance requirements (SOC2, FIPS/HSM, SSO), latency and throughput SLOs, and pilot scope (3 racks). Next steps are to share security docs and installer flow, schedule a technical deep dive, and provide a capacity/cost estimate.
topics: Operational model: control plane in private vs Redwood-managed
transcript:
[00:00] Lena Zhou: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — appreciate you making time. I'm Lena from Redwood, AE for your account. We're joined by Marcus, our SE, and Ivy from CS. How's everyone?
[00:12] Tom Rivera: Hey Lena, thanks. Tom here, CTO at Northstar. We've got Priya, Aaron, Sam and Maya on from our side.
[00:20] Lena Zhou: Perfect. Quick agenda: 1) understand your constraints for an air-gapped on-prem install, 2) security/compliance must-haves, 3) hardware and ops constraints, and 4) next steps. Marcus will dig into technical details. Sound good?
[00:32] Priya Singh: Sounds good. To set context, we run regulated imaging workflows, PHI in scope, and our legal/compliance team requires zero internet egress from the inference cluster — everything has to be fully air-gapped.
[00:44] Marcus Patel: OK, got it. When you say air-gapped, do you mean the inference nodes have no outbound network at all, and updates have to be done manually via signed bundles?
[00:51] Priya Singh: Exactly. Only a jump host in our DMZ can talk to the internet for inbound packages if signed and scanned. We also need HSM-backed key management and FIPS level crypto.
[01:05] Dr. Aaron Lee: From the ML side, our typical request load is chat+generation for clinician note summarization and embeddings for search. We're targeting 95p latency under 250ms for single-turn responses and sustained QPS around 400 queries/minute across peak patterns.
[01:22] Marcus Patel: Right — that's helpful. Two quick clarifying questions: 1) do you already have preferred GPU hardware? e.g., H100 vs A100? 2) Is the control plane allowed to be hosted externally, or does that need to be on your network as well?
[01:35] Sam Ortiz: Control plane has to be inside the private network as well — nothing can call home. We can host the control plane VMs in a management VLAN but still fully isolated.
[01:44] Tom Rivera: For hardware, our data center team prefers Nvidia H100s but we might have a mix. Cooling/power per rack is constrained — roughly 22kW per rack and only 3 racks available for the pilot.
[01:56] Marcus Patel: OK, that helps a lot. Redwood Private supports fully air-gapped installs: we provide an installer bundle that your infra team runs, plus an offline update mechanism. Packages are signed by Redwood and we can integrate with your HSM for master keys. The control plane can be deployed inside your VPC/on-prem and we don't need outbound egress after install unless you opt in for telemetry — which is also off by default.
[02:20] Priya Singh: Can you describe the offline update flow? Our audits require a reproducible process for updates and ability to verify package integrity.
[02:27] Marcus Patel: Sure. The standard flow is: Redwood builds a release bundle, signs it with our signing key, we publish the signature artifact to S3, then you download the bundle onto a staging machine in your DMZ. We provide a verification utility that checks the signature against our public key, then you move the bundle over to the air-gapped environment via approved media. For extra assurance we can co-sign with your key or integrate with your HSM to wrap keys. We also provide checksums and reproducible build metadata.
[02:58] Maya Flores: Do you support detached signatures and timestamping? Our auditors ask for signed timestamps and chain of custody.
[03:05] Marcus Patel: Yes, we can provide detached signatures and TST stamping. We'll add a sample of the signed metadata to the security pack.
[03:12] Dr. Aaron Lee: How about model upgrades — say we want to move from a 7B to a 13B quantized variant — do we have to re-transfer models each time? What's the size and typical downtime?
[03:22] Marcus Patel: Model artifacts are included in the bundle. For large models, transfers are heavy but we support layer-wise delta packages to reduce transfer size if you're staying within compatible format and quantization. Downtime can be zero if you use a blue/green rollout inside the private control plane, but for air-gapped single-cluster installs you might schedule a maintenance window. Typical swap for a 13B quantized model is about 15–40 minutes depending on disk speeds and caching strategy.
[03:45] Tom Rivera: Disk throughput's a constraint for us — we only have roughly 12GB/s aggregate for the pilot racks. Will Redwood runtime be impacted?
[03:53] Marcus Patel: Could be; the runtime relies on fast local NVMe for KV cache and model paging. We'll recommend enough NVMe per node and pre-warm caches during the deploy. We'll put detailed IOPS and throughput numbers in the follow-up capacity doc.
[04:08] Priya Singh: Encryption at rest — does Redwood support customer-managed keys via an HSM? We need to ensure keys never leave our HSM and are FIPS compliant.
[04:18] Marcus Patel: Yes, Redwood Private can integrate with your HSM. Keys for disk encryption and signing can be wrapped by the HSM. We also support bring-your-own-key (BYOK) patterns and can run KMS agents inside your network.
[04:29] Lena Zhou: Quick commercial check — are you evaluating Redwood Hosted or Dedicated at all, or is Private the only option because of the air-gap requirement?
[04:38] Tom Rivera: Hosted is a non-starter because of PHI and the air-gap. Dedicated might be interesting but still needs a private network; ultimately we think Private on-prem will be required at least for the pilot.
[04:48] Marcus Patel: Understood. Two related things to call out: 1) our Private on-prem package includes the control plane, operator, and runtime images; we can support canary rollouts and rollbacks locally, and 2) we can provide a dedicated engineering engagement for the initial install and train your infra team.
[05:05] Sam Ortiz: We'll definitely need that. Our infra team hasn't run the Redwood operator before. Also curious about monitoring: if telemetry is off, how do we still get debug traces during an incident?
[05:16] Marcus Patel: We ship a local observability stack you can keep inside the air-gapped environment: logs, traces, per-route latency breakdowns and token cost estimates. You can expose those to your internal dashboards. If you want Redwood to access traces for support, that's opt-in and uses a secure temporary bundle transfer with explicit approval.
[05:35] Priya Singh: What about RBAC and SSO? We use SAML 2.0 and SCIM for provisioning.
[05:42] Marcus Patel: We support SAML 2.0, SCIM, and LDAP integrations for user provisioning. RBAC is role-based with token scopes. We'll include an RBAC example in the follow-up.
[05:52] Dr. Aaron Lee: From the model side, we care about quantization and latency tradeoffs. Can you run int8 quantized models and what kind of latency improvements should we expect?
[06:00] Marcus Patel: Our runtime supports quantized int8 paths and optimized kernels for both H100 and A100 families. For many decoder-only models, int8 can reduce memory and improve throughput 1.5–2x with a small perf delta in quality — we'll include model-specific perf numbers in the atlas.
[06:18] Tom Rivera: Any constraints around GPU interconnect or NVLink versions? We have mixed nodes and older NVLink bridges on two of the racks.
[06:26] Marcus Patel: We can operate in non-NVLink setups but multi-GPU sharded configs benefit from NVLink. For the pilot, given only 3 racks and mixed hardware, we might recommend per-node sharding rather than across-node sharding to keep things simpler. We'll validate in the capacity assessment.
[06:42] Lena Zhou: Let's talk success criteria: what would make this pilot a go for procurement and compliance?
[06:48] Maya Flores: From compliance: proof of signed offline updates, HSM integration, RBAC and audit logs. From procurement: cost estimate for pilot and roadmap for scaling. From engineering: meeting the 95p latency under 250ms and stability over a 2-week soak.
[07:02] Lena Zhou: Great — we'll map those to deliverables.
[07:06] Tom Rivera: A few other questions: do you provide a hardened OS image and do we need to run our own image signing?
[07:12] Marcus Patel: We provide RESTOREable images that are minimal and we support co-signing. If you require image signing using your signing keys, we can integrate that in the build pipeline so the final images are signed by you.
[07:24] Priya Singh: Audit trails — can logs be exported to our SIEM (Splunk) inside air-gapped network?
[07:30] Marcus Patel: Yes — logs and metrics can be forwarded to an internal endpoint. We ship Fluent or a similar agent that can push to Splunk within your network.
[07:38] Dr. Aaron Lee: A practical question — can we run Redwood runtime on smaller V100-style nodes for cost reasons? Our budget is tight and H100s are expensive.
[07:47] Marcus Patel: You can run on A100s or smaller GPUs but performance and memory will be impacted. We can quantify throughput per GPU type in the capacity doc. For low-cost proof-of-concept, we sometimes recommend mixed nodes with cheaper GPUs for embedding workloads and stronger GPUs for generation.
[08:00] Sam Ortiz: About backups — are model artifacts replicated across racks? We prefer local copies per rack and a replicate-to-offsite plan via encrypted tape for disaster recovery.
[08:09] Marcus Patel: Redwood can replicate model artifacts across nodes and you can snapshot to your chosen backup medium. We'll document recommended snapshot cadence.
[08:18] Priya Singh: Liability — if a signed bundle is compromised, what's the rollback story?
[08:23] Marcus Patel: We keep signed artifacts and release metadata; you can roll back to previous signed versions. We also support image immutability and version pinning so you can freeze a release.
[08:34] Lena Zhou: We're about 8 minutes into the call; want to dive a bit deeper into the update cadence and operator model — Marcus?
[08:40] Marcus Patel: Sure. The operator handles model lifecycle, routing, and batching policies. For air-gapped installs, the operator runs with local images and doesn't attempt to pull from public registries. Update cadence is configurable; many customers run monthly security patches and quarterly model upgrades. For emergency security patches, we provide an expedited signed bundle and can coordinate a maintenance window.
[09:04] Dr. Aaron Lee: On batching — we care about latency vs cost. Can we run per-route SLOs so embedding routes use bigger batches and generation routes keep low latency?
[09:13] Marcus Patel: Yes, per-route configuration is supported. You can set max batch size, latency SLOs, and the smart runtime will respect those with adaptive batching. We'll include suggested defaults for your workload profile.
[09:27] Tom Rivera: Network policy — we have strict egress blocks. Do any agent components try to phone home for licensing?
[09:34] Marcus Patel: No phone-home required. Licensing is handled via signed local licenses in the air-gapped environment. If you choose managed support, secure temporary transfer is used only with explicit approvals.
[09:45] Priya Singh: How long is the typical install engagement? Our ops calendar is tight.
[09:50] Marcus Patel: For a three-rack pilot we estimate a 4–6 week engagement including planning, install, validation and a 2-week soak. We can compress timeline with additional Redwood engineer days.
[09:59] Lena Zhou: We'll capture that in the SOW draft.
[10:02] [10:02] Aaron Lee: Quick run of realistic load — if we send a mix of 40% embedding, 60% generation, peak QPS with short context, what kind of token-per-second throughput should we expect per H100 node?
[10:15] Marcus Patel: Ballpark: an H100 node for this mix might do ~8–12k tokens/s depending on model and sequence length — again model-specific. We'll run microbenchmarks in the pilot and share a spreadsheet.
[10:30] Tom Rivera: Ok. Regarding monitoring retention and privacy — what logs are included by default and what's the retention story?
[10:37] Marcus Patel: By default logs stay local, retention is configurable. For PHI we recommend minimal token-level logging; we have redaction and hashing hooks to avoid storing user content. We'll include redaction examples in the security pack.
[10:53] Priya Singh: Auditors will want to see a runbook for incident response and data exfil attempts. Do you provide templates?
[10:59] Ivy Chen: We do. We have runbooks and incident response templates tailored for on-prem deployments; we'll share examples.
[11:07] Sam Ortiz: One more infra constraint: our racks have limited spare PCIe slots and we need to know physical layout requirements for GPUs and NVMe — can you include a hardware checklist?
[11:16] Marcus Patel: Absolutely — we'll include per-node physical requirements and recommended NIC speeds.
[11:22] Dr. Aaron Lee: For the pilot success criteria, can you commit to latency test scripts or NFR tests we can run to validate performance?
[11:29] Marcus Patel: Yes — we provide a benchmark harness you can run locally; we can also run benchmarks together during the deep-dive so we validate numbers on your hardware.
[11:39] Lena Zhou: Good. We're approaching the last 5 minutes — let's recap next steps. Marcus?
[11:45] Marcus Patel: We'll produce: 1) security pack with SOC2/ISO, HSM/FIPS notes, RBAC examples; 2) air-gapped installer and offline update flow doc; 3) capacity/cost estimate for a 3-rack pilot including GPU recommendations and NVMe/IOPS needs; 4) runbook and benchmark harness. I'll own the installer doc and benchmarks.
[12:06] Tom Rivera: Great. We'll send the rack specs and expected QPS by Monday.
[12:12] Priya Singh: We'll review the security pack and flag any gaps; may request additional attestations.
[12:18] Lena Zhou: Ok, final items: I'll email the SOC2 and our standard SOW template, Marcus will send the installer checklist. We'll schedule the technical deep-dive for next Tue at 11am PT. Anything else?
[12:29] Maya Flores: No, that's it from compliance. Thanks.
[12:33] Tom Rivera: Thanks everyone.
[12:36] Lena Zhou: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the docs and calendar invite.
[12:40] [END]
